abstract: Stem cell-based cartilage regeneration remains constrained by functional heterogeneity and phenotypic drift in conventional cell sources, compromising durable structural repair. Human umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stromal cells (UC-MSCs) represent an accessible, off-the-shelf cell source; however, their broad clinical utility is hampered by cellular heterogeneity, leaving the key chondrogenic subpopulation responsible for cartilage repair unresolved. By integrating single-cell transcriptomics with functional assays, we identified and prospectively isolated a distinct, highly expandable subpopulation of skeletal stem cell-like progenitors (U-CPCs) from the human umbilical cord, establishing an extra-skeletal cell source uniquely primed for joint restoration. Single-cell transcriptomics reveal their inherent regulatory landscape, uncovering a distinct transcriptional state uniquely primed for chondrogenesis. In comparison with conventional stem cells and other tissue-derived SSC-like populations (from umbilical cord, bone marrow, adipose tissue, and dental pulp), U-CPCs exhibit a markedly enhanced chondrogenic capacity. In both a mouse cartilage injury model and a rat osteoarthritis model, the administration of U-CPCs effectively mitigates joint degeneration and drives the restoration of a structurally sound, hyaline-like matrix. Mechanistically, U-CPCs secrete extracellular vesicles enriched with microRNA Let-7a-5p, which specifically modulates DUSP7/MAPK/ERK signaling in recipient chondrocytes, thereby restoring extracellular matrix homeostasis and promoting cartilage repair. By characterizing these specialized extra-skeletal progenitors and elucidating both their intrinsic chondrogenic priming and paracrine regulation of host tissue, this study establishes U-CPCs as a robust, lineage-restricted cellular source for osteoarthritis therapy.
